topic: understanding the concept of the Law of Sines for solving non-right triangles

easy.text: The Law of Sines is primarily used to solve for missing sides or angles in which type of triangle?

options.feedback: Correct -- unlike basic right-triangle trigonometry (SOH-CAH-TOA), the Law of Sines works for ANY triangle, including those without a right angle.
The Law of Sines is actually most notably useful for NON-right triangles -- right triangles can typically be solved using simpler basic trigonometric ratios.
The Law of Sines applies broadly to any triangle type, not exclusively to equilateral triangles (which have their own simple properties).

options.text: Triangles are never applicable for the Law of Sines
options.feedback: This is incorrect -- the Law of Sines is specifically a triangle-solving tool, applicable to any general triangle.

medium.text: The Law of Sines states: a/sin(A) = b/sin(B) = c/sin(C). If angle A = 30°, angle B = 70°, and side a = 10, find side b (rounded to one decimal place). (sin30°=0.5, sin70°≈0.94)

options.feedback: Correct -- setting up 10/0.5 = b/0.94, solving gives b = (10×0.94)/0.5 = 18.8.
This doesn't correctly apply the Law of Sines proportion to solve for the unknown side b.
This appears to invert the correct ratio setup -- check which values go in the numerator versus denominator.
This doesn't correctly result from solving the proportion 10/0.5 = b/0.94.

hard.text: A triangle has angle A = 40°, side a = 15, and side b = 20. Using the Law of Sines to find angle B, why might this particular setup potentially yield TWO possible valid triangles (the 'ambiguous case')?

options.text: Since the sine function gives the same value for both an angle and its supplement (180° minus that angle), solving for angle B might yield two different valid angle solutions, both of which could form a geometrically valid triangle given the other known values
options.feedback: Correct -- this ambiguous case (SSA configuration) is a well-known consideration when using the Law of Sines, requiring careful checking of both possible angle solutions to determine which one(s) actually produce a valid triangle.

options.text: The Law of Sines actually always produces exactly one single unambiguous solution in every possible scenario
options.feedback: This isn't accurate -- certain configurations (specifically, side-side-angle or 'SSA' setups like this one) CAN produce an ambiguous case with two possible valid solutions, not always just one.

options.text: This ambiguity has no actual connection to any mathematical properties of the sine function
options.feedback: This ambiguity is DIRECTLY connected to and caused by a specific mathematical property of the sine function (that sin(θ) = sin(180°-θ)), not an unrelated issue.

options.text: This particular set of given values could never actually form a valid triangle at all
options.feedback: This isn't necessarily accurate -- this configuration might actually produce one or even two valid triangles (the ambiguous case), not automatically zero valid triangles.

hard.hard: Recall that the sine function's periodic symmetry (equal values for supplementary angles) can produce two geometrically distinct, valid angle solutions from a single calculated sine value.
hard.medium: Since sine gives the same number for an angle and its 'flip' (180 minus that angle), there might be two different angles that both technically work.
